blocks.text: The lizard belongs to the eight defiling animals which are called שרצים (§. 269), partly on account of their short feet (like the mouse, weasel, hedgehog and mole), partly on account of their footlessness and hence creeping motion (as is the case with the snail). To the former kind belong our common lizard and, in particular, the lizard species Hardun (§. 274). As already mentioned earlier (§. 270), these eight animals are harmless to man, and indeed even the most snappish lizard does not wound unless it is attacked or provoked.

Like those other animals, it too has a thick (Sabbat 107a), albeit soft and smooth skin (Chulin 122a). It lays eggs (ibid. 122b) in which white and yolk are not separated (A. Sara 40a). The severed tail twitches and continues to move for some time (Erachin 7a); here Raschi says: the severed tail no longer has (actual) life and is nevertheless able to produce the convulsive twitchings; on the other hand, the same author says expressly on Chagigah 11a that there is still life in the severed tail.

But of course there can be no question here of actual sentient life. The convulsive twitchings, which one also otherwise observes in the torn-off legs of spiders, are probably caused by the circulation of the blood remaining in those parts, and they cease only when the blood (or blood-sap) loses the last trace of animal warmth and congeals.

An interesting report is given about the revival of a lizard that was apparently dead. Namely, such a lizard was found in a butcher's stall, in consequence of which the meat would have had to be regarded as defiled. Then R. Gamliel inquired about the temperature of the interior of the premises, and when this was found to be warm, the Rabbi [p. 222] had cold water poured on the lizard, whereby it came back to life, and so the meat was declared usable (Pesachim 88b*). The revival is here called רינחש, which Raschi explains as mere twitching; however, it is well known that frozen salamanders thaw back to life (Voigt l. c. 3. p. 13); Voigt also relates that Hofrath Tilesius in Brazil believed an alligator to have long since been killed and therefore placed it in a jar of spirits, but on the following day it gave such a jerk that it broke the jar.
The lizard, however, can be killed quickly only if a violent blow breaks its spine, whereas otherwise the heart and the severed tail often move for hours.
Sabbat 77b states: The סממית serves against the scorpion's sting. Further: Nature cast upon five great and strong creatures the fear of five weak creatures; thus the scorpion fears the סממית.

Raschi both times translates the word by אייראניאה, Araignée, spider; but Bochart (l. c. 1, 4, 7. col. 1085) rightly remarks that that statement is nowhere found with regard to the spider, whereas it emerges from many parallel passages in ancient works of natural science that the lizard is the most fearsome enemy of scorpions, so that its mere sight makes scorpions rigid. Whether the mentioned remedy against the scorpion's sting is perhaps meant here as a cure by antidote**), or as a means of extermination, in the sense that nature created the lizard for the extermination of scorpions, the expression הק"בה ברא סממית לעקרב, “God created the Semamit against the scorpion,” could well apply to both interpretations.

The only question is how the scorpion can here be called a strong creature and the lizard a weak one; [p. 223] but here (as Bochart l. c. 2, 5, 18. col. 793 remarks) what is meant is not outward size but inner intensive power, since scorpion venom was indeed considered the strongest; cf. also Voigt (loc. cit. 4. p. 114).

Our passage further states: One should take a black and a white סממית, boil them together and smear the wound with them. What is meant here is probably the Lacerta agilis, of which there are green, black and grey ones; the latter two are called Lacertam atram and Lacertam arenicolam (Voigt l. c. 3, p. 39), and these two species are probably meant here, since חיור denotes both pure white and grey colour (cf. Landau s.v. חיור).

- סממית is perhaps identical with שממית. Of the latter it is said (Sanhedrin 103b) that it was brought onto the altar by Amon, who burned the Law and abolished the Temple service. Here too Raschi translates שממית as spider (cf. §. 400); Aruch explains the word as lizard, referring to Jonathan, who renders לטאה in Lev. 11, 30 by שממיתא; yet Raschi's explanation is more acceptable, see §. 400.

This is the name of the lizard widespread throughout the Orient, which in Linnaeus is called Lacerta stellio, in Voigt the Stachelschwanz (spiny-tail), and by which Kimchi explains the Hebrew כח (Lev. 11, 30). It is olive-brown, tending toward blackish, with a spotted back. The tail is ringed black and yellow, and the lizard is one foot long (Voigt l. c. 3. p. 40).
Rosenmüller (loc. cit. 4, 2. p. 260) adds that the back of this lizard is furrowed and scaly. The scales are pointed at the top.
